title: Your Signature Method
overview: This session showed you what turns a good teacher into a recognised authority: a named, memorable method that creates transformation rather than just learning. Vishen told the story of losing the Silva Method business and how writing The Code of the Extraordinary Mind taught him the science of phraseology, then gave you the five practices of transformation that Mindvalley builds into every course, seminar and even physical product.
key_ideas: Vishen's second Beautiful Destruction: in 2014 the Silva Method, 25% of Mindvalley's revenue and a $5 million business he had built over ten years, was taken from him in a court case he could not win. He handed it over, laid off 18 people, and a book marketer who refused to refund a $10,000 fee told him to write a book instead. The first chapter took six months; the final chapter (later made into an Emmy-winning film) took one day. When you understand the process, it gets easier and easier.

That book, The Code of the Extraordinary Mind, earned an $800,000 advance, hit the New York Times list, and every buyer of the $13 to $23 book went on to spend around $550 on Mindvalley products. It led to the course Be Extraordinary, still the highest-rated on Mindvalley nine years on, and five years later the Silva family asked Vishen to become the face of the Silva Method, now Mindvalley's best-selling programme. The lesson: the universe had been whispering 'you should be teaching' for years before it forced the issue.

Phraseology is the science behind the book's success. Each of its ten chapters is a word or phrase Vishen coined and made memorable: culturescape, bullshit rules, consciousness engineering, models of reality, systems for living, bend reality, blissipline, unfuckwithable, Live Your Quest, plus the bonus Six Phase Meditation that became its own book. In November 2017 the book hit number one across all of Amazon, briefly overtaking the combined works of Tolkien. Marisa Peer's Rapid Transformational Therapy is phraseology in exactly the same way.

Vishen engineered the book to be sticky. He dropped the introduction and celebrity foreword (bullshit rules) and opened with 'Before you begin: no, this is not your typical book' and five reasons it was unique. He wrote his own introduction using idea collision - the Dalai Lama and shots of vodka smashed together so you have to keep reading - and told readers the book adds more than 20 new words to English. Amazon only counts a book as read past page 11, and his readers got there while other free Kindle books were dropped by page 7 or 8.

Don't create learning, create transformation. You forget 80% of a book within 24 hours, but transformation is the acceptance of a new meaning schema (University of Toronto): a mind once expanded can never shrink back. After WildFit, Vishen went from 22% to 14% body fat and has stayed there for ten years because he can never eat unhealthily again; after Lifebook you can never again set goals in only one of life's 12 categories.

Transformation is an identity shift. Using James Clear's Atomic Habits, there are three ways to set a goal: outcome (lose 5 kilograms), process (gym three times a week, high-intensity interval training) and identity (I have the body of an athlete and my body needs to move). Outcome goals fail on cold, tired days and process slips from three sessions to two, but identity just is. Most people stop at outcome, better teachers stop at process, great teachers shift identity.

The 5 Practices of Transformation are the ingredient list Mindvalley uses for every course, seminar and this summit: critical reflection, critical study and writing, social discourse, rate of application and altered states. Vishen showed how the summit had already used four of them: the Bob Proctor story and 3MIQ made you question whether your goals are big enough (reflection), he insisted you write on paper (writing), he had you share one goal in the chat (discourse), and he made you do it right then and stick it on your wall (application). Peer-reviewed studies link reflective writing to stress resilience, stronger immunity and emotional wellness.

The practices apply beyond online courses. Marisa Peer's Uncompromised Life (around $25 to $30 million from one course) uses all five, including a hypnotherapy on money blocks delivered in the course with sound technology, fixing in one session what others stretch into 20-session packages. A Harv Eker seminar ran reflection, writing, partner discussion, a commitment and visualisations in one sequence. For a physical product, Vishen's supplement brand uses a free educational e-book with an interactive self-assessment, and designs the product for daily use to raise rate of application; three of the five was enough, and a free e-book once lifted sales 96% overnight.

frameworks.name: Phraseology (how The Code of the Extraordinary Mind was made sticky)
steps: Give each core idea or chapter its own coined word or phrase and make it memorable (culturescape, consciousness engineering, blissipline, unfuckwithable, Live Your Quest).
Drop the standard introduction and foreword; open with 'Before you begin' and the reasons this book is unlike others.
Write your own introduction using idea collision: smash two unlikely ideas together (the Dalai Lama and vodka) so the reader has to know what happens next.
Get the reader past page 11, the point at which Amazon counts a book as read.
Announce the new vocabulary up front so readers want to discover it: 'this book contributes more than 20 new words to the English language'.

frameworks.name: Outcome, Process, Identity (from James Clear's Atomic Habits)
steps: Outcome: the result you want (lose 5 kilograms). Easiest to abandon when you are cold or tired.
Process: the routine (gym three times a week, high-intensity interval training). Better, but slips when life gets busy.
Identity: who you are (I have the body of an athlete, my body needs to move). No longer a habit, it just is. Great teachers move students all the way here.

frameworks.name: The 5 Practices of Transformation
steps: Critical reflection: get the audience to examine an assumption about the world and shift it.
Critical study and writing: have them apply the idea by studying it and writing it down on paper, not just typing.
Social discourse: bring students together to talk to each other about what they learned.
Rate of application: get them to act immediately, not tomorrow.
Altered states: use meditation, hypnotherapy, breathwork or guided visualisation to embed the change.

exercises: Take a photo of the 5 Practices of Transformation slide. This is your design map for your course, event or product.

Ask yourself honestly: are you applying this? Go through critical reflection, critical study and writing, social discourse, rate of application and altered states for whatever you teach, and note which are missing. Even a fitness coach can read a guided visualisation.
Look at the phraseology page Vishen shared from the back of his book and notice how each chapter is a coined phrase; start listing the words and phrases that are uniquely yours.
next_steps: Audit your current course, programme or event against the five practices and add the one or two you are missing this week.
Write down the system you already run with clients and give each step a name in your own words - the beginning of your phraseology.
Rewrite one lesson or session so it ends with an immediate action the student takes right then, not homework for tomorrow.
If you sell a product, draft the outline of a free educational e-book that helps customers reflect on their problem before they buy.
